Selected work

Independent structural study · Solo

Writing a finite-element solver, then using it to kill my own result

Role
Sole author: model, solver, optimizer, report
Duration
May 2026 – present
Tools
MATLAB, fmincon, SolidWorks, Python/SciPy
Status
Conclusion reversed and published; FEA validation in progress

I wrote a 3D-frame finite-element solver from scratch to test whether a joined wing could carry an RQ-4-class UAV at lower structural mass than a conventional wing. My first result said yes. It was wrong, and I found out why myself: I had let the joined-wing spar taper and held the conventional spar uniform. Given the same freedom, the conventional wing is 16% lighter, so I reversed the conclusion and republished.

What I did

  • Wrote the solver in MATLAB from first principles: element stiffness matrices, assembly, constraint handling, and the global solve.
  • Verified it against closed-form beam theory to about one part in 1015, and against an independent Python/SciPy implementation.
  • Added plate-buckling, Euler-column, and combined-stress constraints, and sized the spars with an fmincon mass optimizer whose every bound has a physical justification.
  • Audited my own comparison, found the taper asymmetry, rebuilt the conventional baseline fairly, and rewrote the report around the corrected conclusion.

Where it started

Earlier, a four-person class project took on the same configuration. The CAD and FEA were mine alone: I modeled the joined wing and ran the FEA comparing it with a conventional wing. I also helped a teammate build the physical model, with laser-cut ribs, dowel spars, primer and a chrome finish. A teammate wrote that project's MATLAB geometry optimization; in the solo study above, the MATLAB is all mine. The class FEA showed 59% less tip deflection for the joined wing, but it measured stiffness, not mass, with a whole rear wing added. The solo study asks the mass question under identical rules.

Technical details, assumptions, and known limits

Baseline. Spec-matched to the RQ-4 Global Hawk: 19.949 m half-span, 50.1 m² wing area, NASA LRN 1015 airfoil, four I-section spars in a graphite-carbon composite (E = 134 GPa, ρ = 1600 kg/m³). The conventional baseline is FEA-validated in SolidWorks and treated as locked ground truth: 37,528 psi max von Mises and 78.2 in tip deflection under the sizing load case.

The calibration factor I flag openly. Bare-spar beam theory under-predicts the real wing's stiffness by about 4.7×, because the stressed skin carries a large share of the bending that a hand idealization can't see. I bridge it with I_effective = KAPPA × I_beam, KAPPA ≈ 4.69, calibrated against the validated baseline. It is a calibration factor, not a result, and it needs re-deriving against any new FEA data point before the optimizer is trusted far from this baseline.

What the verification does and does not prove. Matching closed-form beam theory to machine precision is code verification: it proves the solver implements the theory correctly. It is not physical validation. Physical validation is the SolidWorks FEA step, which is in progress.

Where the model stops. A two-node beam element cannot compute plate buckling; the frame solve returns internal forces and local buckling is a post-processing check on the section geometry using classical coefficients. Fatigue, aeroelasticity, plasticity, and joint detail are unmodeled. Most of those shift both configurations in the same direction, and where there is an asymmetry it works against the joined wing, whose slender rear tie and structural joint are more connection- and aeroelastically-sensitive than a clean cantilever. Refining the model can reinforce “no advantage,” not rescue the original claim.

Rensselaer Motorsport · Accumulator sub-team

Keeping water out of a Formula SAE high-voltage pack

Role
Design engineer: lid and sealing interface
Duration
Oct 2023 – Dec 2024
Tools
SolidWorks, GD&T, sheet metal, DFM
Status
Delivered to the team build

I designed the lid and sealing interface for the team's high-voltage accumulator: a ¼″ compressible gasket on a lip at the container wall, clamped by positive-locking over-centre latches. I chose them over quarter-turn latches because a seal is only as good as the preload holding it, and an over-centre latch keeps a defined preload through vibration. The lid is a five-piece 0.040″ 4130 weldment the team could build and inspect in-house.

What I did

  • Compared quarter-turn and over-centre latch concepts on whether they hold gasket preload, not just whether they hold the lid shut.
  • Detailed the lid as a bent top with four welded lip flanges, and made the corner an explicit choice between a welded sharp corner and a bent radius.
  • Traded rivnuts against welded latch mounts: rivnuts blocked segment install, so welding won on packaging, at a cost in heat and distortion.
  • Flagged the open risks at design review: the container lip the seal depends on, and midspan bow between latches eating into the foam's travel.
Technical details

Why the latch is a sealing decision. A compressive gasket only seals while it is held compressed. A quarter-turn latch is compact and tool-free but its clamp load depends on how far it is turned and how the catch is set; an over-centre compression latch carries a defined preload and stays there through vibration, which is the failure mode that matters on a race car.

Bowing between the latches. The latches clamp the left and right sides, which leaves the span between them free to bow, and 0.040″ sheet is not stiff. On a compressive seal a bow at midspan comes straight out of the gasket compression. Closing it is a deflection number checked against the travel left in the ¼″ foam, and it is still open.

What welding the latches costs. An over-centre latch holds its preload through a spring-tempered element, and weld heat in the wrong place anneals that temper. The larger cost is distortion: 0.040″ sheet moves when you weld it, and the flatness of the sealing flange is what keeps gasket compression even around the perimeter. Weld distortion and midspan bow draw on the same budget, the travel left in the foam.

Fluid Dynamics Lab, RPI · Four-person team

What flap deflection actually does to lift, drag, and pitch

My contribution
Results & discussion: data reduction, analysis, interpretation
Duration
Jan 2026 – May 2026
Rig
2′×2′ low-speed tunnel, 6-component sting balance, LabVIEW VI
Team
Four students; I authored the analysis

Our team tested a Stingray UAV model in RPI's 2′×2′ low-speed wind tunnel at 150 ft/s (Re ≈ 4.0 × 105), sweeping angle of attack from −4° to 18° across three flap settings. I owned the results and discussion, reducing the sting-balance loads into lift, drag, and pitching-moment coefficients and working out what they meant. The finding: 20° of down-flap raised CL,max from ≈ 0.68 to ≈ 0.80, at the cost of the highest drag of the three configurations and a more nose-down moment, while 25° of up-flap cut lift enough to go negative at low α and flattened the pitching-moment slope toward reduced static stability.

What I did

  • Resolved the balance's native axial and normal loads into wind-axis lift and drag using the measured angle of attack, then non-dimensionalized on the model's 50.27 in² planform area.
  • Analyzed lift-curve behaviour across all three flap settings, identifying how camber change moves the zero-lift angle of attack in each direction.
  • Built the drag polar, and flagged its scatter as uncertainty-dominated rather than presenting it as a precise measurement.
  • Interpreted the pitching-moment slope as a static-stability statement, and corroborated the force data against the flow visualization instead of trusting either alone.

Why it mattered

Flap deflection is a cheap way to buy lift and an expensive way to buy drag and a pitching moment you then have to trim out. Characterizing all three together across the deflection range is what turns “flaps help” into a design decision someone can size a tail and a control-authority budget against, and the up-flap case is the one that matters most, because it buys descent authority by spending stability margin.

Technical details, and where this data should not be trusted

Setup. RPI 2′×2′ low-speed tunnel with a Mini 6-component sting balance; a LabVIEW VI logged balance loads, angle of attack, and tunnel speed while α and speed were set manually. Sensors were re-zeroed before every configuration to remove electrical drift and the model's own gravitational and static-moment bias. The model spans 12 in with a 4.125 in mean chord, giving S = 50.27 in².

Frame transformation. The balance reads axial (A) and normal (N) force in its own frame, so lift and drag come from L = N cosα − A sinα and D = N sinα + A cosα.

The drag polar is the weakest result and I said so. Drag forces here are far smaller than lift, which makes them disproportionately sensitive to alignment error, balance resolution, zeroing drift, and the coordinate transform itself. The polar shows real scatter at low CL, so it belongs in the report as a qualitative comparison of trends, not as a precise measurement.

What the flow visualization does and does not corroborate. The bubble probe forced the visualization runs down to roughly 15 ft/s, an order of magnitude below the force-balance condition, so it confirms the trends (attachment, separation at the flap hinge, wake thickness), not behaviour at the same Reynolds number. The 25° up configuration was never visualized at all, for time; its flow behaviour is inferred from the force data, and I've kept that inference labelled as one.

Current & more work

In progress · RPI Hacking for Defense · USSOCOM

A quiet airframe for a Group 2 drone

USSOCOM's problem: drones that are radio-silent but can still be heard. The target is a Group 2 payload at Group 1 noise. On the fuselage-and-wing team, I'm laying out an airframe that keeps the propeller in clean air: a twin-boom pusher with the hub raised above the wing wake, a portal-frame motor mount in place of a single post that would resonate near shaft frequency, and carbon spar and booms sized around the blade-pass band.

Airframe work is mine; the propeller and thrust come from the propulsion team. Final review Dec 8.

In progress · Intro to CFD · Team of two

Validating a CFD model before trusting it to cool avionics

Forced-air cooling of an avionics heat sink in Altair AcuSolve. We validate one fin passage first against Shah & London's laminar solution across three flow rates, then add the aluminium fins and base for a conjugate heat-transfer sweep of thermal resistance against fan power.

Every part split 50/50 between the two of us. Final report Nov 19.
